texto_en: There is no single official figure for ‘neurodivergent people worldwide’. Major international organisations do not use neurodivergence as a homogeneous statistical category: they measure specific conditions, disability, functioning, support needs, diagnosis, identification or social participation.

This section brings together figures that can be cited with precision. Each page states what was measured, in whom, where, when and using which source. When two figures seem contradictory, the first step is to check whether they are really measuring the same thing.

Autism · modelled global prevalence, differences in identification, diagnosis and comparison between countries. ADHD and learning · childhood and adult ADHD, dyslexia, coordination, Tourette syndrome, language, dyscalculia and dysgraphia. Mental health · anxiety, OCD and coexistence with autism. Disability and childhood · health, education, wellbeing, discrimination and access to support. Work and income · employment, labour-force participation and pay gap. European Union · employment, education, training, poverty and discrimination. Countries · United States, United Kingdom, Australia and Canada with national official sources. Methodological comparison · how to read international figures without creating false rankings.

A high or low figure does not, by itself, mean that a condition is more or less common in a country. It may change because the age studied, access to diagnosis, available records, the definition, the survey or the statistical method change. That is why each page keeps its context and explains what should not be concluded from it.

The main sources are WHO, UNICEF, ILO/ILOSTAT, Eurostat, CDC, GOV.UK, the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the Public Health Agency of Canada and selected international scientific reviews from the underlying research base.
Last editorial review of this document: 1 September 2026.
Each `PAGE` block can become an independent page within the Data tab.
Always keep territory + population + year of the data + method + source together.
Do not add together prevalences of neurodivergent conditions: there is overlap between them.
Do not use disability as a synonym for neurodivergence.
Do not turn figures about children into figures for the whole population.
Do not mix registered diagnosis, identification, survey data, meta-analysis and modelled prevalence.
Do not round or change denominators unless the entry itself says so.
Mental health figures appear because they are part of the knowledge base and may coexist with neurodivergent conditions; they are not presented as a synonym for neurodivergence.

In 2021, an estimated 61.8 million people —approximately 1 in every 127— were autistic worldwide. This is a modelled estimate from Global Burden of Disease 2021, not a count of diagnoses. WHO currently uses this figure and notes that observed prevalence varies widely between studies and remains unknown in many low- and middle-income countries.
2021 · 2025; WHO updates the fact sheet in 2025.
2025; WHO updates the fact sheet in 2025
The Global Burden of Disease 2021 study estimated 61.8 million autistic people worldwide, with an uncertainty interval of 52.1 to 72.7 million.
Global age-standardised prevalence was estimated at 788.3 per 100,000 people.

The figure attempts to estimate autism prevalence across all ages worldwide through epidemiological modelling. It can therefore approximate populations where no complete diagnostic register exists, but it should not be confused with the number of diagnoses issued by health or education services.
Cite it as a modelled global estimate, not as a count of diagnoses. Keep together 61.8 million, 1 in 127, the year 2021 and the GBD/WHO reference.

The previous GBD 2019 estimate was much lower. The study itself explains that a significant part of the difference is due to methodological changes, including no longer relying on passive-identification studies that may have underestimated prevalence. The jump between GBD 2019 and GBD 2021 should therefore not be presented as a real increase in autism in just two years.
Autism: sex differences in the global estimate

The GBD 2021 global model estimated 1,064.7 autistic people per 100,000 males and 508.1 per 100,000 females. These are modelled epidemiological estimates and are not equivalent to the proportion of diagnoses recorded by health or education services.
Every 2 years or when GBD changes
GBD 2021 estimated a modelled prevalence approximately twice as high in males as in females.

The comparison uses age-standardised rates from the same global model. It is useful for observing an estimated difference between males and females and, when compared with higher diagnostic ratios, for showing that identification and prevalence are not exactly the same thing.

Diagnostic ratios are often higher than this modelled difference. A review of 54 studies and more than 13.7 million participants found that the male:female ratio was 4.20:1 when all studies were pooled, but fell to 3.25:1 in studies that screened the general population instead of starting only from already existing diagnoses.
This is compatible with identification bias: diagnostic figures do not measure prevalence alone.
Always state that the sex-specific rates are age-standardised modelled estimates. Do not present them as a global diagnostic ratio or as a closed biological difference.
The figure must remain linked to its population, territory, year and method. Separating it from that context can change its meaning.

In 2021, the Global Burden of Disease model estimated 11.5 million DALYs associated with autism. This measure is used to study population-level health burden; it does not describe the experience, quality of life or individual needs of an autistic person.
Every 2 years or when GBD changes
GBD model population for 2021, not a count of people
GBD 2021 estimated that autism accounted for 11.5 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) in 2021.

DALYs are a measure of population health burden. They are used to compare conditions within GBD models; they do not indicate how many years a specific person loses, nor do they summarise quality of life, autonomy, support needs or strengths.

A DALY is a measure of population health burden. It does not mean that an autistic person literally ‘loses’ a specific number of years of life. It combines years of life lost due to premature mortality and years lived with disability according to the GBD model.

For autism, this figure must be used very cautiously because it depends on the model’s disability weights and does not describe strengths, individual quality of life or the specific needs of a person.
If the DALY figure is used, explain what a DALY is. Do not translate it into ‘years of life lost for each autistic person’ and do not use it as an individual measure of quality of life.
The figure must remain linked to its population, territory, year and method. Separating it from that context can change its meaning.
